implementation_notes: Java mud is common because the build tool will happily accept it: a few Maven modules that depend on each other through a shared `common` or `core` jar, or one application jar that is every module's dependency. The compiler forbids class-level cycles, so the mud shows up as wide module dependencies and a fat `core` artifact. Consolidation is well-supported by tooling here — JPMS/`module-info.java` makes the export graph explicit and will reject a cycle at compile time, which is the strongest enforcement available in any language in this catalogue. Diagnose with `mvn dependency:tree` or `jdeps`.
idiom_name: Maven module graph with near-total overlap; one God service jar
pitfalls: `provided`/`test` scopes can hide a real runtime dependency from `dependency:tree` output that developers read.
Spring's component scan removes the compile-time dependency on a service and replaces it with a runtime bean lookup, so the mud becomes invisible to `jdeps`.
A single fat `core` jar is usually the whole problem; moving to JPMS only helps if the exports, not just the packages, are narrowed.
